prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of GLP-1 and the identity of its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us placed B006 first, but unanimity is not itself the argument. The argument is that this is a complete discovery arc: proglucagon processing and the identity of the active truncated GLP-1, its glucose-dependent insulinotropic action in humans, the broader biology of satiety, gastric emptying and tissue actions, and then therapies validated by large independent randomized outcome trials in diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal disease. Originality, mechanistic clarity and scale of benefit are all very high, and the maturity question is settled; if anything the field is overdue. A physiology-centred prize with three names is the configuration that best protects the science.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Priority for identifying the active GLP-1(7-36) form is contested between Mojsov and other groups, Habener is not among the credited names, and any physiology-only trio leaves out the industrial design work (acylation, half-life extension) that actually produced liraglutide and semaglutide. If the committee judged that the drug-development step is inseparable from the benefit to humankind, my configuration would be too academic. I also note that a three-person cap forces a choice that the historical record does not make clean.

responses.point: Proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, arguing that Knudsen's long-acting acylated analogues are what made the drug class real, and treating Mojsov as disputed.
responses.response: I take the point that without half-life extension there is no therapy, and I do not dismiss Knudsen. But the prize's strongest claim rests on discovery of the physiology and the active peptide, and the committee would be rewarding an industrial program with many contributors on one name while leaving out the peptide identification. I would accept Knudsen over Mojsov only if the committee decides that the verifiable record of the active-peptide work is too uncertain to credit; I do not think that has been shown from what we have.

responses.point: Leans to Drucker, Holst and Knudsen to span physiology and translation, while admitting Mojsov and unlisted contributors such as Habener are a real allocation problem.
responses.response: I agree that spanning physiology and translation is attractive and that the allocation problem is real. My disagreement is narrow: a translational slot filled by one company scientist is an arbitrary representative of a collective effort, whereas the active-peptide identification is a discrete, citable discovery. I would want the chair to ask for documentary evidence on the Mojsov and Habener priority question before we settle between the two trios.

responses.point: Ranks B039 (Walter and Mori) second as a clean, fundamental cell-biology discovery with no obvious omission among the credited names.
responses.response: I agree that B039 has the cleanest attribution on the shortlist and that it resembles fundamental cell-biology prizes. Where I qualify his view is on disease relevance: the UPR link to diabetes and neurodegeneration is real but the therapeutic payoff (ISRIB, PERK inhibitors) is still early, and Ron, Kaufman and Kozutsumi on the other arms are not trivially excluded. That makes it my first alternative rather than a competitor for this year's main prize.

responses.point: Ranks CAR-T second and cGAS-STING fourth, stressing recalled priority disputes and that CAR designers beyond the credited trio (Eshhar and others) are omitted.
responses.response: His concern about omitted CAR pioneers is serious and I share it: Eshhar's chimeric receptor concept being outside the credited names makes any B004 trio hard to defend, which is why I place it only as a second alternative. I differ on cGAS-STING, which he ranks above B039: its mechanism is clean, but with no approved therapeutic yet I would wait.

responses.point: Ranks cGAS-STING third and notes that therapeutic translation of STING agonists and inhibitors has been disappointing, so recognition would rest on mechanism.
responses.response: I agree that cGAS-STING would be a mechanism-only recognition at present, and that is precisely why I rank it below B039, whose mechanism is equally established and whose organelle-to-nucleus signalling concept is more general. I do not think the committee needs to rush it; further clinical evidence would strengthen the case.

uncertainties: Whether the verifiable record supports crediting Mojsov for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide over Knudsen, and whether Habener's omission from the credited names is acceptable.
Whether the committee wants to reward physiology, drug design, or both, given the three-person cap.
I am relying on recalled history for priority questions and have not verified them from primary documents.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My documented scientific connections (single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, and co-authors such as Sandberg, Frisen and Betsholtz) do not involve any shortlisted candidate or credited name.
